newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian finance minister tackles investors' worries.
newsitem.headline: Indian finance minister tackles investors' worries.

text.p: India's Finance Minister P. Chidambaram sought to reassure sceptical foreign businessmen on Tuesday that the centre-left government is pressing ahead with economic reforms while tightening the nation's budgetary belt.
Chidambaram told the World Economic Forum that he was confident the government would meet both its fiscal deficit and economic growth targets for the 1996/97 financial year that began on April 1.
He read out a long list of steps that Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government has taken since assuming office in June to open the economy to private investment, including foreign money.
"We have not been idle in the last four and a half months," he told the forum's conference on its second and last day.

"This period compares very favourably with the first four and a half months of the Narasimha Rao government," he said, referring to former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, who launched India's economic liberalisation policies in 1991.

Chidambaram defended the 13-party ruling coalition a day after Deve Gowda told the forum -- made up of leading foreign businessmen and political leaders -- that his government was committed to welcoming foreign investment and spurring growth.

Both leaders were addressing growing doubts about whether the disparate coalition, which ranges from communists to free traders, can keep a lid on red ink, meet an ambitious growth target and roll back restrictions on foreign investment.

Both former French prime minister Raymond Barre and World Economic Forum managing director Claude Smadja outlined the anxieties in addressing the conference. The finance minister replied with a vigorous defence of the government's policies.
Chidambaram said he was determined to meet the goal of cutting the fiscal deficit, or total net government borrowing, to five percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from 5.9 percent in 1995/96.

"Nobody believes I will do that. But I am confident we will keep the fiscal deficit at five percent," he said. "There is no reason to believe that this government has given up its goal of containing the fiscal deficit."
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank have urged India to cut the deficit to help reduce interest rates and spur growth.
Chidambaram said he expected the government to achieve its target of seven percent annual GDP growth over the medium term by implementing the broad policy agenda it drew up in June.
GDP grew 6.3 percent in 1995/96, and the government has set a tentative growth target of 6.6 percent for 1996/97. Many economists claim the target will be tough to meet.

Chidambaram acknowledged that currently "there is a slight slowdown". But he said industrial production was expanding at an annual rate of more than eight percent, and predicted agriculture production would touch a new peak this fiscal year.
"With the reduction in real interest rates, I expect the economy to pick up," he said, referring to a recent credit easing by the central bank.

The finance minister said the government had cleared more than $4 billion in foreign direct investment proposals, opened up the mining sector, extended financial guarantees to three large foreign power projects and adjusted petrol and coal prices.
